\title{What Belongs in an Agent's Context Window?}

\author{Neil Lunavat}
\affiliation{%
  \institution{Pimpri Chinchwad College of Engineering}
  \country{India}}
\email{neillunavat3192@gmail.com}

\begin{abstract}
An LLM coding agent works inside a finite context window, and before it edits a file of an
unfamiliar repository it must choose what else to put there. Given the file being changed, we
compare the two signals tools use for that choice --- proximity in the import graph and the
words of the issue report --- and their fusion, on 2{,}412 change tasks from 1{,}162 pull
requests in 112 Python repositories, scoring each reading order by how much of an answer key it
covers per line read.

Our main contribution is a measurement protocol. Benchmarks built from issue reports mix two
regimes, because in two tasks in five the issue names a file the change touches. Stratifying
by that naming, comparing against an issue-free twin of each ordering, and deleting only the
names from the same issue separates them. Applied here, it shows the issue is worth $+0.156$
AUC to the best ordering where it names a key file against a non-significant $+0.016$
elsewhere, and that about half of that difference is the naming itself; a dense code retriever
reads the issue better but leaves the structure intact. Under the same controls the apparent
contest between graph and text dissolves, and a key annotated by people sides with the
patch-derived key the field already uses. The practical recommendation is to fuse a walk from
the file with issue retrieval: it held under predictions committed before scoring on seven
unseen repositories and on the human-annotated key, and when the file to change must itself be
guessed. Everything here runs without paid model access; we specify, but do not run, the
end-to-end agent experiment.
\end{abstract}

\keywords{LLM agents, context windows, code search, context retrieval, dependency graphs, benchmark validity, empirical
software engineering}

\maketitle

\section{Introduction}

An LLM coding agent is handed a bug report and a file to change. Before it can write anything
it must decide what else to put in its context window, and it cannot simply include everything. In the corpus we study the
median pull request is made against a repository of 286{,}385 tokens --- counting the
Python files in the import graph, excluding tests and non-Python files --- and 74.8\% of pull
requests are made against a repository larger than a 128{,}000-token window. The files that
carry the answer are a median 2.98\% of the repository. Something has to choose.

Two signals are available. The dominant one in tool building is the dependency graph: Aider
builds a repository map from definitions and references, and RepoGraph, LocAgent and CoSIL
walk a code graph outward from a starting point, on the premise that what you need is near
what you are changing. The other is the issue report, which SWE-bench's own retrieval
baseline queries with BM25~\cite{jimenez2024swebench} and which every agent reads. We compare
the two, and their fusion, as \emph{reading orders} scored by how much of an answer key they
cover per line read. Every task hands the reader the file being changed; the question is what
\emph{else} to read. We measure retrieval, not repair.

A naive version of this comparison is easy to run and misleading. Graded against the files
co-edited in the pull request, issue text wins; graded against the files defining symbols the
change uses, structure wins, and the method ranking nearly inverts. Neither half survives two
controls. The structural half is a population effect: a symbol key exists for single-file
changes and a co-edited key does not, so the two are scored on different pull requests. The
lexical half is largely the issue naming the answer: in two tasks in five the issue names a
changed file as code, which a method matching issue words against file paths can simply read.
A key annotated by people then sides with the co-edited key.

What survives is two findings, and the paper is organised around them. The first concerns
the benchmark more than the methods. Issue-aware retrieval is worth far more on issues that
name their files, and a within-task redaction experiment measures how much of that is the
names themselves. We call the names \emph{leakage} only in this benchmark sense: in
deployment an issue that names \texttt{core.py} is a legitimate input, but an average over
issues that do and do not describes neither, and the mix varies by corpus. The second is a
recommendation: fusing a walk from the file with issue retrieval is robust across keys,
strata, unseen repositories, a human-annotated key, alternative cost rules and the loss of the
free seed, except for single-file changes, where the walk alone is better.

\paragraph{Research questions.}
\begin{description}
\item[RQ1] Does the uncontrolled comparison of structural and lexical reading orders survive
matching the populations and controlling for issues that name the answer?
\item[RQ2] What is issue text worth to retrieval, and how much of it is the issue naming the
files to change?
\item[RQ3] Which ordering is robust, and does it hold on unseen repositories, a
human-annotated key, other cost rules, and without a free seed?
\item[RQ4] What, beyond that, does the import graph contribute?
\end{description}

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A protocol for measuring what issue text is worth.} An issue-free twin of each
ordering gives the issue's total value, and three nested within-task redactions give the part
carried by what points at the key files. On issues that name a key file as code the issue is
worth $+0.156$ AUC to the best fusion, of which $0.061$ to $0.078$ is attributable to the names;
on the rest it is worth $+0.016$. A dense retriever reads the issue better but the structure
is the same (Section~\ref{sec:issue}).
\item \textbf{A robust recommendation, tested out of sample.} Reciprocal-rank fusion of a
personalised walk with issue retrieval is never significantly worse than the best pure
ordering on the matched population, held under predictions committed before scoring on seven
unseen repositories and on ContextBench's human-annotated key, and remains best without a
free seed. Whether the walk should favour short files depends on how a context is charged
(Section~\ref{sec:robust}).
\item \textbf{Controls that changed conclusions here}: matching the populations two keys are
scored on; stratifying by whether the issue names a key file as code; and the repository as
the unit, which leaves the headline comparisons significant but changes the significance
verdict on 102 of the 1{,}076 comparisons significant with the pull request as the unit
(none changes sign).
\item \textbf{Corrections to common arguments for graph retrieval.} The two-hop
neighbourhood holds on average 87.5\% of the needed files and 56\% of the repository. Walking against
import edges is costly, discarding direction is not. And the advantage structure shows on a
key built from imports is not corroborated by a human-annotated key (Section~\ref{sec:graph}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Structure and history as guides to change.} Impact
analysis~\cite{bohner1996impact} propagates from a changed element along dependencies;
Robillard~\cite{robillard2008topology} ranks program elements by dependency topology;
feature-location surveys~\cite{dit2013featurelocation} note that structural, textual and
dynamic techniques are usually evaluated in isolation; and Ko et
al.~\cite{ko2006exploratory} observed developers navigating largely by names and search.
Co-change mining~\cite{zimmermann2004mining,ying2004predicting} suggests files that change
together; our co-edited key uses that notion as ground truth rather than as a method.

\paragraph{Graph-based context for agents.} SWE-bench~\cite{jimenez2024swebench} and its
successors~\cite{badertdinov2025swerebench,zhang2025swebenchlive} made repository-scale
change tasks a standard benchmark, and a family of systems assembles context by walking a
code graph: Aider's repository map~\cite{aider2023repomap}, RepoGraph~\cite{ouyang2025repograph},
LocAgent~\cite{chen2025locagent} and CoSIL~\cite{jiang2025cosil}; Agentless~\cite{xia2025agentless}
leans on file and directory names instead. Table~\ref{tab:priorkeys} records what each is
graded against, read from its own evaluation section. Almost all use the files touched by the
gold patch --- our co-edited key --- and our results support that choice: of our two proxies it
is the one a human-annotated key agrees with. What none of them reports is its results
separately for issues that do and do not name the files being scored.

\paragraph{Issues that give the answer away.} SWE-Bench+~\cite{aleithan2024swebenchplus} finds
that 32.67\% of the patches SWE-Agent with GPT-4 gets passed had the solution in the issue or
its comments, and Agentless reports issues containing the exact patch. A weaker form concerns
only \emph{where}: a retrieval step needs only to know which files to open. This too is known.
Agentless classifies the location information in SWE-bench Lite and finds that around half of
its issues already provide the location of the file to be edited, and the SWE-Bench Illusion
study~\cite{liang2025illusion} shows that models name the buggy file from the issue alone in
up to 76\% of SWE-bench Verified tasks against 53\% on repositories outside SWE-bench. Our rate,
40.2\% of tasks naming a key file as code, is in line with the first. What we add is not the
rate but its consequence: how much of an issue-aware method's score it accounts for, separated
within task from the rest of what the issue says.

\paragraph{Concurrent work on the key.} SWE-Explore~\cite{zhang2026sweexplore} derives ground
truth from code that successful agents read and scores ranked lists under a line budget, close
to our cost model; ContextBench~\cite{li2026contextbench} annotates gold context by hand;
AgentRetrievalBench~\cite{qin2026agentretrievalbench} scores files by whether they help the next
step; GraphLocator~\cite{liu2025graphlocator} dual-annotates the patch key. We use
ContextBench's key as a third, independent answer key (Section~\ref{sec:robust}).

\section{Study Design}
\label{sec:design-freeze}

The corpus, graph builder, task definition and metric were fixed and tagged in version
control before any method was run (the \emph{design freeze}); the method families, the fusion
among them, were added afterwards in response to the first results, so the fusion began as an
exploratory result. We then tested it twice under predictions committed to the repository
before any of the data they concern were scored (\texttt{paper/external\_predictions.md},
\texttt{paper/contextbench\_predictions.md}). A signed tag in our own repository establishes
order only to a reader who trusts the repository; we do not call either step a
pre-registration. Analyses added in response to review and not fixed in advance --- the cost
rules, the dense retriever, the systems' selectors and the condition without a free seed ---
are marked exploratory where they appear, and every change made after results existed is logged
in the replication package.

\subsection{Corpus, tasks and keys}

\begin{sloppypar}
We drew 1{,}886 pull requests from SWE-bench, SWE-bench-Live and SWE-rebench in Python
repositories that pass our sampling rules, at most 20 per repository. A pull request that edits
$k$ existing non-test source files that are nodes of the import graph yields $k$ tasks: each
edited file in turn becomes the \emph{seed}, and the task is to order the remaining files of
the repository. This gives 3{,}123 tasks from 1{,}873 pull requests in 113 repositories (13
pull requests edit no graph file). Of these, 2{,}412 tasks --- 1{,}162 pull requests in 112
repositories --- have at least one key file once the seed is removed, and they are the ones
scored. Of the 711 unscored tasks, 706 come from pull requests changing a single source file;
they are 61.2\% of all 1{,}154 such tasks, because the symbol key below is empty whenever the
changed code resolves to nothing outside itself. The median task's repository has 131 graph
nodes and the median key 2 files.
\end{sloppypar}

Graphs are built per base commit with an \m{ast} walker: nodes are source files, an edge
$a \rightarrow b$ means $a$ imports a module resolving to $b$, test files are excluded, and
per-file line counts from the same pass are the cost unit. Two keys, never merged:

\begin{description}
\item[\m{co\_edited}] The other non-test source files changed by the same pull request: what
a developer in fact touched, independent of the import graph. Available only when a pull
request edits more than one graph file: 1{,}958 tasks from 708 pull requests.
\item[\m{symbol}] Files defining names used on the lines the pull request adds, resolved by
\texttt{jedi}'s \texttt{goto} with \texttt{follow\_imports=True} on the patched code: what the
change depends on. 2{,}341 tasks from 1{,}156 pull requests.
\end{description}

\noindent The symbol key is built by following imports, so it is partly circular with the
structural orderings, and we treat it as the secondary proxy. The 702 pull requests carrying
both keys form the \emph{matched population}, on which every cross-key comparison is repeated.
Of the 1{,}156 pull requests with a symbol key, 454 have no co-edited key because they edit a
single graph file; we call these \emph{single-file} pull requests. By \emph{issue text} we mean
the problem statement only, not maintainers' \texttt{hints\_text}.

A third key, used only in Section~\ref{sec:robust}, is ContextBench's human-annotated gold
context~\cite{li2026contextbench}: the Python files a person judged necessary to reconstruct
the fix, less the seed. We ran its SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro Python tasks through
the unchanged pipeline, drawn by our sampling rules: 108 pull requests in 14 repositories have
a non-empty gold key, 6 of them also in the main sample.

\subsection{Reading orders}

Every ordering receives the graph, the seed, per-file identifier bags and the issue text, and
ranks every other file (Table~\ref{tab:methods}). Identifier bags split identifiers on
underscores and camel case; the issue is tokenised the same way. BM25 uses $k_1 = 1.5$,
$b = 0.75$ and differs between methods only in the query. Fusion is reciprocal-rank fusion
(RRF) with $k = 60$. Variants suffixed \m{\_pl} divide a score by file length. Four
orderings recur, and in the text we use plain names for them: \emph{the fusion}
(\m{rrf\_pprpl\_issue\_path}), \emph{the length-aware walk} (\m{ppr\_und\_pl}), \emph{the hop
walk} (\m{hops\_lines}) and \emph{path matching} (\m{path\_issue}). Structural
orderings are handed a correct seed; issue orderings get no seed at all.

Three further kinds of ordering were added after review and are scored but kept out of the
ranks and correction families of the other tables, so that adding them moves nothing
reported elsewhere. A \emph{dense retriever}, \texttt{jina-embeddings-v2-base-code} --- the model
our design fixed before any method ran --- ranks files by cosine similarity of their first 512
tokens to the issue (\m{dense\_issue}), which is embedded whole as the length-weighted mean
of its 512-token chunks; its fusions replace or join BM25 over contents. The \emph{issue-free
twins} of the fusions replace every issue-derived input by its seed-derived counterpart. And
the \emph{context selectors of three published systems} --- Aider's repository map, RepoGraph's
two-hop ego graph and LocAgent's typed breadth-first search, reimplemented from their papers
--- are scored as orderings, with the files they do not select appended in random order.

\subsection{Metric}

An ordering is read from the top, whole file by whole file, until the next file would exceed
the line budget. Coverage is the fraction of the key read. We evaluate at budgets of 250 to
32{,}000 lines in doublings and report the AUC, the mean coverage over the eight budgets; ties
are re-drawn three times and averaged. Python source runs to 8.50 tokens per line in
aggregate over the 121{,}075 distinct file versions (\texttt{cl100k\_base}), so a budget of
8{,}000 lines is roughly 68{,}000 tokens. Restricting the AUC to budgets up to 8{,}000 lines
leaves the leading orderings unchanged.

AUC has no intuitive scale, so we anchor it. On the matched population a random ordering
scores 0.249 and the oracle 0.774 on the co-edited key (0.252 and 0.779 on the symbol key), so a
difference of 0.05 AUC is about a tenth of the distance from random to oracle; the recommended
fusion covers 45\% of that distance on the co-edited key and 41\% on the symbol key. We also
report lines read before half the key is covered (Table~\ref{tab:lines} in the appendix).

The rule that reading stops at the first file that overflows the budget is part of the frozen
metric. Because it favours short files, Section~\ref{sec:robust} also scores every ordering
under a rule that skips such a file and continues, and under one that charges each file one
unit whatever its length.

\subsection{Statistics}
\label{sec:stats}

Task AUCs are averaged within a pull request first. Paired comparisons use the Wilcoxon
signed-rank test with the repository as the unit --- pull-request scores averaged within each
of the 112 repositories --- because pull requests cluster in repositories that differ in size,
layout and issue-writing culture. Effect sizes are Vargha--Delaney $A_{12}$; confidence
intervals bootstrap over repositories. Holm correction is applied within families fixed by the
design (Table~\ref{tab:families}): each key, unit, population and leakage stratum is one family
of 325 tests among twenty-six orderings. Ranks are among the twenty-two ranked orderings, the oracle excluded, so the best ordering
is first. Differences quoted in the text are from the repository-level Wilcoxon analysis:
means of per-repository differences, which can differ in the third decimal from the
pull-request means in tables. The mixed-model estimates of the same comparisons are in
Table~\ref{tab:mixed} and can differ slightly from them.

The unit matters for borderline comparisons: of the 1{,}076 comparisons significant after
Holm correction with the pull request as the unit, 102 are not with the repository as the unit
and 2 move the other way; no estimate changes sign. Every comparison a claim rests on is also
re-estimated as a linear mixed model of the per-pull-request difference with a random
intercept per repository (Table~\ref{tab:mixed}); on 40 of those 41 comparisons it reaches the
same verdict. The exception is the hop walk against path matching on co-edited files,
where the mixed model finds path matching better by 0.044 ($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-3}$) and the
repository-level test does not; no claim rests on that comparison being null.

\section{Results}

\subsection{RQ1: the naive comparison, and why it does not survive}
\label{sec:naive}

Table~\ref{tab:main} is the comparison as it is usually run: each key over its full
population, no control. Under the co-edited key the five best orderings are four
fusions and one lexical method; the best purely structural ordering is ninth. Under the symbol
key the four best orderings are three structural orderings and one fusion, and the
best lexical ordering is fourteenth. The individual reversals are large and significant:
path matching beats the length-aware walk by 0.059 AUC on co-edited
files ($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-4}$) and loses to it by 0.100 on symbol files
($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-7}$). Read naively, the choice of key decides which signal wins.

\paragraph{The structural half is a population effect.} The two columns are scored on
different pull requests: 454 of the symbol column's pull requests are single-file changes,
which have no co-edited key and are exactly where a seed's import neighbourhood is most of
what there is to find. On the 702 pull requests carrying both keys (Table~\ref{tab:shared}),
nothing moves on the co-edited key, while on the symbol key a walk along import edges falls
from first to seventh (0.491 to 0.417) and path matching rises from fourteenth to eighth. The
same comparison that gave the walk a 0.101 lead on the full corpus ($p_{\text{Holm}} <
10^{-7}$) gives $+0.008$ and $p_{\text{Holm}} = 1$ on the matched population; for
the hop walk against path matching it gives $+0.019$ and $p_{\text{Holm}} = 1$. The three top
places under both keys are then held by the same three fusions.

\paragraph{The lexical half is largely the issue naming the answer.} A key file's full path
appears verbatim in the issue for 12.6\% of tasks and its bare stem for 48.5\%. A stem written
as code --- \texttt{core.py}, \texttt{simbad/core}, a dotted module path, inside backticks or
a code block --- we call an \emph{explicit} mention; one written only as an ordinary word, an
\emph{incidental} one. Explicit mentions cover 40.2\% of tasks. Removing them, together with the
population control (Table~\ref{tab:leak}), takes path matching on co-edited files from fifth
to twelfth and pure structure from ninth to fifth; the hop walk over path matching goes
from $-0.007$ under the full-path control ($p_{\text{Holm}} = 1$) to $+0.042$ under the primary
control ($p_{\text{Holm}} = 0.60$), on 531 pull requests. The ordering that looked like the best
single signal on this key becomes indistinguishable from one that never reads the issue. The
issue does not name the seed file more often than the key files, so the seed is not the
explanation: its full path appears in 10.3\% of tasks.

\paragraph{Which proxy to believe.} Where the two keys still disagree, a key annotated by people
decides. On ContextBench's tasks it sides with the co-edited key: the ranking under the human
key agrees with the co-edited key's at Kendall $\tau = 0.97$ and with the symbol key's at 0.59,
and the length-aware walks that are first and fourth under the symbol key are tenth and
fourteenth under the human one (Table~\ref{tab:cbauc}). So the answer to RQ1 is no: once the
populations are matched and the naming is controlled, neither signal family dominates, and the
key the field already uses is the better of the two proxies. The rest of this section asks
what, then, the issue is worth, and which ordering is safe.

\subsection{RQ2: what the issue is worth, and how much is the names}
\label{sec:issue}

Stratifying by whether the issue names a key file compares two kinds of issue as well as two
degrees of leakage: a report containing a stack trace is plausibly longer and more tractable
than a one-line feature request. We therefore measure the issue's value twice, once across
tasks and once within them.

\paragraph{Across tasks: an issue-free twin.} Each fusion is paired with a twin in which every
issue-derived input is replaced by its seed-derived counterpart: \m{rrf\_pprpl\_issue\_path}
with \m{rrf\_pprpl\_seedpath}, which fuses the same walk with the same two BM25 rankings queried
by the seed's own path and contents. The twin blends the same number of lists and never reads
the issue, so the difference is what the issue is worth, net of ``a fusion just gets more
input''. On the matched population the issue is worth $+0.069$ AUC to the fusion on the co-edited
key and $+0.055$ on the symbol key. On the tasks whose issue names a key file as code that
becomes $+0.156$ and $+0.121$; on the rest, $+0.016$ and $+0.012$, and neither survives
correction.

\paragraph{Within task: redaction.} We then take the \emph{same} issue and delete what points
at the key files, leaving the prose, the traceback and the length. What counts as ``pointing''
is a choice, so we make it three times. The \emph{names} arm deletes only explicit mentions of
the key files' stems; the \emph{paths} arm also deletes every component of their paths; the
\emph{symbols} arm also deletes every function, class and method name they define, each only
where written as code. The names arm is a lower bound on leakage; the wider arms over-remove,
since a directory called \texttt{models} is also ordinary vocabulary, so the three bracket the
effect. Of the 970 tasks whose issues name a key file, the 848 in the matched population ---
378 pull requests in 105 repositories --- are scored. Removing just the names costs
path matching 0.110 AUC on co-edited files and the fusion 0.061; the wider arms cost the
fusion 0.084 and 0.096 (Table~\ref{tab:decomp}). On the issues that name nothing the names arm
changes nothing, as it must, while the wider arms cost 0.016 to 0.018 there, which is the part
they over-remove.

\paragraph{The decomposition.} Both experiments run on the same population with the same unit,
so they add up. On issues that name a key file the issue is worth $+0.156$ to the fusion on
co-edited files; on the rest, $+0.016$. Of that $+0.140$ gap the names arm attributes $0.061$
to the names; the widest arm, net of what it also removes where nothing is named, attributes
$0.078$ (on the symbol key, $0.050$ to $0.065$ of a $+0.109$ gap). So between two fifths and a
half of the difference between the two kinds of issue is the naming itself, and the rest is a
difference between the issues, or the tasks, that no redaction we could define reaches: even
path matching, which reads only file paths, scores 0.393 on named-file tasks after the widest
redaction against 0.333 elsewhere.

\paragraph{A better reader.} Everything above reads the issue with BM25, so ``what the issue is
worth'' could describe the retriever rather than the issue. The dense retriever reads it
better: alone it beats BM25 over contents by 0.059 and 0.054, and in place of BM25 in the
fusion it adds 0.018 on both keys (Table~\ref{tab:dense}). On issues that name nothing, the
dense fusion gains 0.033 from the issue on co-edited files, twice what the BM25 fusion gains
and, unlike it, significant; on the symbol key it gains 0.017, not significantly. So part of
the small value of unnamed issues was BM25's. But it is still a fifth of what the same fusion
gains where the issue names a file, 0.178, and the names account for a similar share: of the
0.145 stratum gap, 40 to 47 per cent against 43 to 56 per cent for BM25. We did not test a
reader that takes in the issue as a whole, such as an LLM reranker; the redaction protocol
applies to one unchanged.

\paragraph{What this licenses.} Not that issue text is useless: an ordering that exploits a real
report naming a real file exploits something that exists. What it shows is that a benchmark
assembled from issue reports measures two regimes at once, in proportions that vary by corpus,
and that they can be separated for the cost of a few regular expressions and one extra run.
Any evaluation on SWE-bench-derived data that reports a gain from issue-aware retrieval without
the stratum and the redaction reports their sum.

\subsection{RQ3: a robust ordering, and how far it travels}
\label{sec:robust}

If the answer key is not known in advance --- for a tool shipped to users it is not --- the
quantity to optimise is the worst a method does across keys, measured as its shortfall behind
the best ordering under either key. On the matched population the best on that
criterion is the fusion, the best ordering under both keys, which
beats the best pure lexical ordering by 0.055 and 0.067 and the best pure structural one by
0.097 and 0.039. It is never significantly worse than the best pure ordering in any leakage
stratum on the matched population. On the full symbol-key population it is: once issues that
name a key file are removed, the length-aware walks beat it by 0.049 to 0.062
($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-4}$), because that population keeps the single-file pull requests. On
those, the five best orderings are all structural, and for a change that touches
one file the walk alone is the better choice.

The fusion was found after seeing results, so we tested it. Table~\ref{tab:robust} collects
every test; Table~\ref{tab:pred} gives the eight predictions committed before scoring.

\paragraph{Held-out repositories.} Across 200 random 56/56 splits of the repositories, a
mechanical criterion applied to one half selects the fusion in 198, and in 195
of those it is the best ordering on the co-edited key of the other half, 198 of 198
on the symbol key (Table~\ref{tab:heldout}). This shows the choice is stable across our
repositories, not that it generalises.

\paragraph{Seven unseen repositories.} Seven repositories pass all our sampling rules and were
left out only because their tasks come from SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Pro. We drew 140 pull
requests from them by the same rules and committed four predictions before building anything.
Three hold: the fusion is second under both keys, behind only
another fusion built on the hop walk, with a worst shortfall of 0.030 --- at the limit we set, not inside
it --- it is never significantly worse than a pure ordering, and walking inward is as costly as
in the main sample. The fourth fails: deleting the names costs the fusion 0.030 on the co-edited
key with $p_{\text{Holm}} = 0.11$, on only 33 matched pull requests in six repositories, so the
causal effect of the names alone is not established there. The wider arms cost 0.086 and
0.090: in these larger repositories issues point at files through their directories more
than their names.

\paragraph{A human-annotated key.} On ContextBench's tasks all four predictions hold. The fusion
is the second-best ordering on the human key, 0.009 behind a fusion of the same
family, and beats each of four named pure orderings by 0.086 to 0.128 ($p_{\text{Holm}} \le
0.008$). Its annotators worked from the fix, and 108 pull requests is a small set, but it is
the only key in this paper that no part of our pipeline built.

\paragraph{Other cost rules.} Under the frozen rule, preferring short files is close to a
knapsack heuristic for the metric, so the length-aware walk could owe its place to the rule.
Under a rule that skips a file that does not fit and keeps reading, the fusion is the best
ordering on the symbol key and 0.002 behind the fusion built on the hop walk on the
co-edited key; but the margin length-awareness buys shrinks by about sixty per cent (the two
fusions differing only in it separate by $+0.015$ and $+0.021$ instead of $+0.042$ and
$+0.050$). Under a rule that charges each file one unit, length-awareness is a cost, and the
unscaled fusion \m{rrf\_ppr\_issue\_path} is best under both keys. A fusion is the best
ordering under every rule; whether its walk should favour short files depends on
whether a context is charged by size, as a token window is, or by the number of files opened
(Table~\ref{tab:metric}).

\paragraph{Without a free seed.} An agent is not handed the file to change. For each pull
request we let the issue pick the seed --- the top file of the dense retriever --- walk from
that guess and fuse, scoring against every edited file (the true seeds included, so that
finding the file is part of the task) and against the symbol key. The guess is the right file
in only 34\% of pull requests, but walking from it and fusing with the dense reader is the best
ordering under both keys, at 0.516 and 0.475 (Table~\ref{tab:seedless}). It beats the dense
retriever alone by 0.023 on the edited files ($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-3}$) and 0.058 on the
symbol key, and ties it where the issue names no edited file ($-0.001$). Seeding the walk with
a BM25 guess instead, right in 41\% of pull requests, does worse: the reader that picks the seed
should be the one that reads the issue in the fusion.

\paragraph{Published systems' selectors.} Scored as orderings on the matched population, the
context selectors of Aider, RepoGraph and LocAgent rank between tenth and twentieth. The
recommended fusion beats each by 0.115 to 0.176 on co-edited files and 0.084 to 0.155 on symbol
files ($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-4}$). Aider's repository map and RepoGraph's two-hop ego graph
also fall below the plain length-aware walk; LocAgent's typed search ties it on co-edited files.
These are the selectors alone, reimplemented from the papers without the language model each
system wraps around them, so the comparison says what their graph component contributes as a
reading order, not how well the systems perform.

\paragraph{The fusion's own parameter.} RRF's $k$ was fixed at 60 without testing; at $k = 10$
and $k = 200$ the fusion's AUC moves by at most 0.007 on the co-edited key and 0.010 on the
symbol key.

\subsection{RQ4: what the import graph contributes}
\label{sec:graph}

\paragraph{The two-hop neighbourhood is half the repository.} 86.7\% of symbol-key files and
88.1\% of co-edited files lie within two undirected hops of the seed (Table~\ref{tab:distance}),
which reads as strong evidence for graph retrieval. But the median two-hop ball holds 68 files
and about 21{,}600 lines, more than five times a 4{,}000-line budget; measured against its own
repository it is a median 58.5\% of it (a mean of 56\%), with a median precision of 3.4\%, and it lifts recall
over a random sample of the same size by a factor of only 1.57. It is not a filter: it says the
files you need are somewhere in half the repository, which is where the \emph{ordering}
decides everything.

\paragraph{Direction: reversing a walk is costly, discarding it is free.} Walking along import
edges, towards what the seed depends on, places \m{ppr\_out\_pl} first on the symbol key at
0.491; walking against them collapses to 0.277, twentieth, a gap of 0.215 on the full
population ($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-14}$). The undirected walk loses almost nothing (0.489).
On the co-edited key every directed walk ranks below \m{same\_dir}, which consults no graph at
all. The symbol key is built by resolving names along imports in one direction, so a walk in
that direction measures something close to the key's construction.

\paragraph{How much is a repository prior.} A query-independent PageRank, which never looks at
the seed or the issue, reaches 0.410 on symbol files against 0.491 for the best personalised
walk --- 67\% of the walk's margin over random --- but only 0.271 on co-edited files, barely
above random (0.248), where the walk beats it by 0.101. Knowing which file is changing matters
a great deal for predicting what else was changed and much less for what the code calls.

\paragraph{The signals find different files.} At $k = 20$, 24.4\% of co-edited files are found
only by the lexical family and 9.5\% only by the structural family; on symbol files the
asymmetry flips (20.0\% against 16.5\%, Table~\ref{tab:comp}). This complementarity is why
fusing them works; where the issue names a key file, much of the lexical side's share is that
naming (Section~\ref{sec:issue}).

\paragraph{What the human key says about the graph.} On the gold files a fix reads but does
not edit --- the context a graph walk is supposed to be best at finding --- walks and issue-only
retrievers are indistinguishable on ContextBench's 85 pull requests that have any (differences
of 0.006 to 0.012, $p_{\text{Holm}} = 1$), and the fusion beats the issue-only orderings by
0.082 and 0.084 ($p_{\text{Holm}} \le 0.008$). This analysis was added after the predictions
were scored.

\paragraph{The budget is rarely the constraint.} An oracle fits the complete key within
8{,}000 lines for 97.5\% of pull requests, where the best ordering completes 58.5\% on the
co-edited key and 51.0\% on the symbol key (Table~\ref{tab:full}). The oracle reads only key
files, so the forty-point gap is an upper bound on what better ordering could add, not an
estimate; what it establishes is that an ordering that fails to cover the key at this budget
fails because of the order.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{For benchmarks.} The field's default key, the files the gold patch touched, is the
better of our two proxies: a human-annotated key agrees with it, not with the key built from
imports. The field's omission is elsewhere. Two tasks in five in this corpus have an issue that
names a key file as code, and an issue-aware method's score mixes that regime with the other.
The control costs a regular expression over text the benchmark already ships; the redaction
costs one extra run. We think retrieval results on issue-derived benchmarks should report the
naming rate, the stratified result and the redaction, as routinely as the corpus size.

\paragraph{For tools.} Fuse a walk from the file being changed with issue retrieval, read the
issue as well as you can --- a dense retriever beats BM25 here --- and make the walk favour short
files only if the context is charged by size. For a change confined to one file, the walk
alone is the better choice. Without a known file, let the same reader pick the starting point.
The two-hop neighbourhood is not a useful filter on its own, and direction matters only in
that walking against imports is costly.

\paragraph{What the baselines do not show.} Our orderings are deliberately simple --- BM25,
PageRank, one embedding model --- and the systems' selectors are reimplemented from their
papers, not run end to end. A skeptic can read the fusion result as two weak complementary
signals beating each alone. We agree that is what it is; its value is that it is robust, cheap
and survives every test we could devise. The methodological contribution does not depend on
it: the stratification and redaction protocol applies to any reader of the issue, including an
LLM reranker, which we did not test.

\paragraph{Scope, and what remains.} Every experiment in this paper runs on a CPU without paid
model access, and within that budget we went as far as we could: two proxy keys, a human key,
unseen repositories, a dense retriever, three systems' selectors, and a condition without the
free seed. What it cannot show is whether better retrieval raises the rate at which an agent
resolves the issue. That needs model calls at scale, and Appendix~\ref{sec:protocol} specifies
the experiment in advance so that it can be run as it stands. Its analysis would inherit the
protocol this paper introduces --- stratifying by naming, the issue-free twin, the redaction,
the repository as the unit --- which is the contribution we offer here.

\paragraph{Recommendations.} (1) Report retrieval results per answer key, and prefer the patch
key to an import-derived one. (2) Report and stratify by whether the query names the answer
files as code, and run the redaction for whatever reads the issue. (3) Compare an issue-aware
method against the same method with a seed-derived query. (4) Match populations before comparing
across keys. (5) Cluster tests by repository. (6) State how reading is charged.

\section{Threats to Validity}
\label{sec:threats}

\paragraph{Construct.} Neither proxy key is ground truth about what a developer needed to read.
The co-edited key conflates files changed with files read; the symbol key is circular with the
structural orderings; the human key covers 108 pull requests and records what the fix needed
as reconstructed by annotators who saw it. Coverage assumes whole files are read; the
alternative cost rules show which conclusions depend on that.

\paragraph{Internal.} The graph builder misses dynamic imports and plugin registration. The
symbol key inherits \texttt{jedi}'s resolution failures, which depend on the environment:
rebuilding the keys of all 1{,}886 sampled pull requests on a second machine left every
co-edited key identical but changed the symbol key of 41 pull requests, usually by one file.
Re-scoring moves no AUC by more than 0.003 and changes no conclusion; in the held-out splits
of Section~\ref{sec:robust} the fusion is then selected in 194 of 200 splits instead of 198, and
confirmed on the co-edited key in 191 of those instead of 195. The paper reports the keys as first built.
The leakage classifier is a regular expression and will mislabel some mentions, which is why we
report three nested strata and three redaction arms. Leakage we did not think to redact --- a
paraphrase of a function's behaviour --- would sit in the residual, so the leakage share is
bounded below more firmly than above.

\paragraph{External.} Python only, file granularity only, and pull requests from benchmarks
that select for reproducible test-verified fixes, which may be better documented than average
and so flatter issue-text methods. Very large repositories are under-represented; the pattern
of Table~\ref{tab:main} is stable across size quartiles (Table~\ref{tab:size}). The external
set is seven repositories and one of its four predictions failed.

\paragraph{Conclusion.} The fusion family was chosen after seeing results. The held-out splits,
the external repositories and the human key test it, but none undoes that it was chosen by us,
from five candidates, on these data.

\section{Conclusion}

What belongs in an agent's context window, given the file it is changing? Compared naively, import-graph
proximity and issue-text matching trade places depending on the answer key. That reversal is
the comparison, not the signals: one half is the different pull requests the two keys cover,
the other the issues that name their files, and a human-annotated key sides with the key the
field already uses. What survives is a protocol and a recommendation. Issue-aware retrieval is
worth $+0.156$ AUC where the issue names a changed file against a non-significant $+0.016$
elsewhere, and about half of that difference is the naming itself; benchmarks should report the two regimes separately. And fusing a walk
from the file with issue retrieval is robust --- across keys, unseen repositories, a human key,
cost rules and the loss of the free seed --- except for single-file changes, where the walk
alone is better.

\section*{Data Availability}

The replication package contains the graphs, tasks, keys, issue bags, orderings and scores; the
external and ContextBench trees with the predictions committed before they were scored; the
scripts that compute the dense embeddings, which are regenerated rather than shipped; and every
analysis script. A checker recomputes every number quoted in the text from the result files
and fails if any sentence disagrees. It will be archived at a permanent identifier on
acceptance.

\section*{Use of AI Tools}

Claude (Anthropic) was used to write the analysis and method code, to run the experiments and
to draft this manuscript. All numbers are produced by scripts in the replication package and
checked mechanically against the text; the author verified the design, the claims and the text.
Bibliographic entries were checked against arXiv and publisher listings, and the evaluation
section of every system in Table~\ref{tab:priorkeys} was read directly.

\section{A Protocol for the Downstream Test}
\label{sec:protocol}

Whether a context assembled by one of these orderings lets a model fix the issue requires
running models, which we have not done; we specify the experiment here so that it can be run
or contradicted. \emph{Corpus}: the 1{,}162 scored pull requests, each with a benchmark test
specification. \emph{Conditions}, each truncated to the same token budget of 16{,}000 or
64{,}000 tokens: (i) the seed alone; (ii) seed plus \m{ppr\_und\_pl}; (iii) seed plus
\m{path\_issue}; (iv) seed plus the recommended fusion; (v) seed plus \m{rrf\_hops\_path};
(vi) seed plus the issue-free twin of (iv); (vii) the repository in a fixed canonical order;
(viii) seed plus the key files, an upper reference. \emph{Models}: two of clearly different
capability, one API call per task and condition, no tools. \emph{Outcome}: a task is resolved
if the patch applies and the specified tests pass; conditions are compared with a mixed-effects
logistic regression with a random intercept per repository, McNemar tests alongside, Holm
across condition pairs. \emph{Pilot}: 150 tasks on the weaker model; if (viii) resolves under
10\% or over 90\%, the budget is adjusted and the adjustment reported. If (ii)--(vi) do not
differ from (vii), retrieval quality does not transfer to repair at these budgets; if (iv) does
not beat (vi), the issue does not earn its place downstream either.

\end{document}
